c.tagline: Rio's tropical escape hatch — a bay of 365 islands, jungle-fringed beaches, and Ilha Grande just a boat ride away.

taxi.fareNote: Metered in town; boat trips and island transfers are negotiated flat fares, not metered

emergency.note: 190 reaches military police, 192 reaches SAMU (ambulance); response can be slow on the islands

hood_landmark.Centro Histórico: Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Conceição
hood_landmark.Praia do Frade: Praia do Frade, Angra dos Reis

avoid.reason: Avoid the hillside favela communities around the mainland town, especially after dark, due to gang-related crime.
Watch for petty theft around the ferry docks, bus station, and beaches, and avoid walking the mainland town center late at night.

hood_desc: Angra's original town center, built around a 16th-century church and a small historic core that survived the city's industrial and naval-shipyard growth. It's the transport hub for buses, the town market, and ferries out to the bay, with a modest walkable strip of shops and eateries.

The car-free village on Ilha Grande, reached only by boat, and the jumping-off point for the island's famous trails and beaches like Lopes Mendes. Sandy paths, pousadas, and seafood shacks replace streets and cars here.
A quieter residential beach neighborhood just outside the center, popular with families and known for its calm bay waters. Fewer tourist crowds than the historic center, with a laid-back, local feel.

A gated hillside resort community and marina on the Rio-Santos highway (BR-101) about 13 km east of Angra's centre, above the beaches of Vila Caetés. Best suited to travellers who want a quiet condo-resort base with a car rather than a walkable town.

A quiet resort stretch on the Rio-Santos highway about 13 km west of Angra's centre, where the Frade and Porto Frade condominiums back a sheltered beach. It holds the Fasano resort, the most expensive hotel in the city, and suits travellers who want a resort base rather than a town.

water.note: Stick to bottled or filtered water, as locals generally do not drink from the tap.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am-11pm; boat schedules vary by season and tide
transit.pay: Cash onboard buses; boat tickets and tours purchased at pier kiosks
transit.map: No official transit app; schedules posted at the Jacuecanga and Centro piers
transit.note: Boats (barcos/escunas) are the main way to reach Ilha Grande and the bay's other islands

air: Angra dos Reis Airport (AIA) - small, very limited traffic
bus: Long-distance coaches from Rio's Novo Rio bus station, ~2.5 hours via Costa Verde highway
ferry: Ferries and schooners to Ilha Grande, Vila do Abraão, and other bay islands

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often already included in restaurant bills; additional tipping isn't expected but rounding up is appreciated

landmarks: Ilha Grande
A car-free jungle island paradise reached by ferry from Angra, where the laid-back village of Vila do Abraao gateways rainforest trails and hundred-plus beaches.
Praia de Lopes Mendes
Regularly ranked among Brazil's most beautiful beaches, three kilometres of squeaky-white sand and jade surf backed by untouched Atlantic forest on Ilha Grande.
Lagoa Azul (Blue Lagoon)
A dazzling turquoise anchorage between islets off Ilha Grande, where schooner day-trippers snorkel among clouds of striped sergeant-major fish.
Ilhas Botinas
Twin forest-tufted islets rising like green boots from gin-clear water, Angra's postcard snorkelling stop on every boat tour itinerary.
Ilha da Gipoia and Praia do Dentista
The bay's playground island, where yachts raft up off Dentista beach for caipirinhas served straight to swimmers in the shallows.
Convento de Sao Bernardino de Sena
Atmospheric hilltop ruins of a 1758 Franciscan convent, their weathered stone arches framing views over Angra's historic centre and island-studded bay.
Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora da Conceicao
Angra's mother church, founded in 1626 on the central square, its baroque interior anchoring the colonial old town by the waterfront.
Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Carmo
A graceful 18th-century church and former convent whose azulejo-trimmed facade recalls Angra's prosperous colonial port days.
Cais Santa Luzia
The bustling waterfront pier where schooners, fishing boats, and Ilha Grande ferries come and go against a spectacular backdrop of 365 islands.
Mirante do Morro do Santo Antonio
A hilltop viewpoint above town unfurling the full sweep of the emerald Bay of Ilha Grande, its islands scattered like stepping stones.

train.note: No railway serves Angra dos Reis, and Brazil has no intercity passenger trains. The coastal BR-101 road is the only land route in. Arrive by coach or car from Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo.

bus.note: No international coaches. Costa Verde runs frequent buses along the coast road from Rio de Janeiro's Rodoviária Novo Rio in about three hours and on to Paraty; Reunidas Paulista covers São Paulo in around six. Book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/). The bus terminal is a short walk from the ferry jetty.

intl.to: Abraão, Ilha Grande (Brazil) - ~80 min from the Cais de Santa Luzia
Ilha Grande & Ilha da Gipoia (Brazil) - faster schooners and lanchas
intl.op: local boat operators — tickets at the pier

ferry.note: There are no international sailings, but the boats to Ilha Grande are the whole reason most people come here. The CCR Barcas ferry is the cheap, slow option from the town pier; private lanchas do the same run in about 25 minutes for more money and go more often. Departures from Conceição de Jacareí, 30 minutes down the coast, are the quickest crossing of all. Services are cut back in rough weather.

half.name: Paraty
half.blurb: Preserved colonial Portuguese port town with cobblestone streets and whitewashed churches on the Costa Verde.

full.name: Rio de Janeiro
full.blurb: Brazil's iconic coastal metropolis, home to Christ the Redeemer and Copacabana beach, a couple hours up the coast.
